(function loadGSAP() {
  if (typeof gsap !== 'undefined') { document.dispatchEvent(new Event('gsap-ready')); return; }
  var savedDefine = window.define;
  window.define = undefined;
  var s1 = document.createElement('script');
  s1.src = 'https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/gsap/3.12.5/gsap.min.js';

<style>
/* Scoped styles for the Poisson MLE theater. Global .gs-theater rules remain shared. */
.gs-theater-pm .gs-screen {
  min-height: 560px;
  overflow: hidden;
  padding: 1.5rem;
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
.gs-theater-pm .gs-scene-wrap {
  display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center;
  width: 100%; height: 100%; padding: 18px 22px; box-sizing: border-box;

}

}

  flex: 1 1 auto; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  width: 100%; min-height: 0;
}

/* Scene 1 */
.pm-soft-wrap { display: inline-flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; gap: 12px; position: relative; }
.pm-soft-box {
  width: 220px; height: 140px;
  border: 2.5px solid #2c3e50; border-radius: 10px;
  background: #faf6ef; transform: rotate(-2deg);
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  font-family: 'Kalam', cursive; font-size: 2rem; color: #2c3e50;
  box-shadow: 4px 6px 0 rgba(44,62,80,0.08);
  position: relative;
}
.pm-soft-box::after {
  content: ''; position: absolute; top: -6px; left: -6px; right: -6px; bottom: -6px;
  border: 1px dashed rgba(44,62,80,0.25); border-radius: 12px; pointer-events: none;
}
.pm-bubble {
  position: relative;
  background: rgba(184,148,90,0.15);
  border: 1.5px solid #b8945a;
  border-radius: 18px;
  padding: 14px 22px;
  font-family: 'Kalam', cursive; font-size: 1.4rem; color: #2c3e50;
  max-width: 420px;
  transform-origin: bottom left;
}
.pm-bubble::after {
  content: ''; position: absolute; bottom: -10px; left: 28px;
  border-left: 10px solid transparent; border-right: 10px solid transparent;
  border-top: 10px solid #b8945a;
}
.pm-bubble::before {
  content: ''; position: absolute; bottom: -8px; left: 30px;
  border-left: 8px solid transparent; border-right: 8px solid transparent;
  border-top: 8px solid rgba(184,148,90,0.15);
  z-index: 1;
}

/* Scene 2 */
.pm-firmgrid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(50, 1fr);
  gap: 3px;
  width: 100%; max-width: 720px;
  margin: 0 auto;
  aspect-ratio: 50 / 30;
}
.pm-firmcountlabel { font-family: 'Kalam', cursive; color: #2c3e50; font-size: 1.4rem; }
.pm-firmtile {
  background: #2c3e50;
  border-radius: 1px;
  aspect-ratio: 1 / 1;
  width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}
.pm-firmcallout {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px;
  margin-top: 14px; font-family: 'Kalam', cursive; color: #2c3e50; font-size: 1.4rem;
}
.pm-firmcallout-tile { width: 28px; height: 28px; background: #2c3e50; border-radius: 4px; }

/* Scene 3 */
.pm-bars { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 18px; width: min(560px, 92%); margin: 0 auto; }
.pm-bar-row {

}

}

/* Scene 4 */
.pm-panel-row { display: flex; gap: 22px; align-items: stretch; justify-content: center; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.pm-panel {
  background: #faf6ef; border: 1px solid rgba(44,62,80,0.18); border-radius: 10px;

}

/* Scene 5 */

}

}

}

/* Scene 6 */
.pm-firm-examples { display: flex; gap: 16px; justify-content: center; flex-wrap: wrap; margin-top: 20px; }
.pm-firm-ex {
  display: grid; grid-template-columns: auto auto auto; align-items: center; gap: 10px;

}

/* Scene 8 */
.pm-counter-wrap { display: flex; gap: 30px; align-items: flex-start; justify-content: center; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.pm-counter-col { display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; gap: 8px; }
.pm-counter-label { font-family: 'Kalam', cursive; color: #2c3e50; font-size: 1.4rem; }
.pm-counter-grid {
  display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(6, 18px); gap: 4px;
}
.pm-counter-cell { width: 18px; height: 18px; border-radius: 3px; background: transparent; }

}

/* Scene 9 */
.pm-verdict-badge {

.pm-final-line {

}
.pm-scroll-arrow { color: #b8945a; font-size: 2rem; }

}
</style>

<script>
function initPmTheater() {
  var hasGsap = typeof gsap !== 'undefined';
  var screen = document.getElementById('gs-screen');
  var tlFill = document.getElementById('gs-tl-fill');
  var prevBtn = document.getElementById('gs-prev');
  var nextBtn = document.getElementById('gs-next');
  var counterEl = document.getElementById('gs-counter');
  var restartBtn = document.getElementById('gs-restart');
  var currentScene = 0;

  function clearScreen() {
    if (hasGsap) gsap.killTweensOf(screen.querySelectorAll('*'));
    screen.innerHTML = '';
    screen.style.opacity = 1;
  }
  function wrap(act, title, contentHtml, caption) {
    return '<div class="gs-scene-wrap">' +
      (act ? '<div class="gs-act-tag">' + act + '</div>' : '') +
      (title ? '<h2 class="gs-scene-title">' + title + '</h2>' : '') +
      '<div class="gs-stage">' + (contentHtml || '') + '</div>' +
      (caption ? '<p class="gs-caption gs-pm-cap">' + caption + '</p>' : '') +
    '</div>';
  }
  function fadeWrap() {
    if (!hasGsap) return;
    gsap.from('.gs-scene-wrap', { opacity: 0, duration: 0.5, ease: 'power1.out' });
    gsap.from('.gs-pm-cap', { opacity: 0, y: 8, duration: 0.5, delay: 0.6, ease: 'power2.out',
      onComplete: function() { gsap.set('.gs-pm-cap', { clearProps: 'transform' }); } });
  }
  function tickCount(targetId, finalVal, decimals, dur, delay) {
    if (!hasGsap) {
      var el = document.getElementById(targetId);
      if (el) el.textContent = Number(finalVal).toFixed(decimals);
      return;
    }
    var obj = { v: 0 };
    gsap.to(obj, {
      v: finalVal, duration: dur || 1.0, delay: delay || 0, ease: 'power2.out',
      onUpdate: function() {
        var el = document.getElementById(targetId);
        if (el) el.textContent = obj.v.toFixed(decimals);
      }
    });
  }
  function typeText(targetId, text, dur, delay) {
    var target = document.getElementById(targetId);
    if (!target) return;
    target.textContent = '';
    if (!hasGsap) { target.textContent = text; return; }
    var prox = {};
    gsap.to(prox, {
      duration: dur || (text.length * 0.025), ease: 'none', delay: delay || 0,
      onUpdate: function() {
        var p = this.progress();
        target.textContent = text.substring(0, Math.floor(p * text.length));
      },
      onComplete: function() { target.textContent = text; }
    });
  }
  function drawPath(selector, dur, delay) {
    var nodes = document.querySelectorAll(selector);
    if (!hasGsap || !nodes.length) return;
    nodes.forEach(function(p, i) {
      var len = (p.getTotalLength ? p.getTotalLength() : 200);
      p.style.strokeDasharray = len;
      p.style.strokeDashoffset = len;
      gsap.to(p, { strokeDashoffset: 0, duration: dur || 0.8, ease: 'power2.inOut',
        delay: (delay || 0) + i * 0.08 });
    });
  }

  // ====================== SCENES ======================
  var scenes = [];

  // Scene 1
  scenes.push(function() {
    var content =
      '<div class="pm-soft-wrap">' +
        '<div class="pm-bubble">Our software helps you get more patents approved!</div>' +
        '<div class="pm-soft-box">Blueprinty</div>' +
      '</div>';
    screen.innerHTML = wrap('ONCE UPON A TIME', 'A small company, a big claim', content,
      "Blueprinty's marketing team has a story. The question is whether the data agree.");
    fadeWrap();
    if (hasGsap) {
      gsap.from('.pm-soft-box', { scale: 0.7, opacity: 0, duration: 0.6,
        ease: 'back.out(1.7)', delay: 0.3,
        onComplete: function() { gsap.set('.pm-soft-box', { clearProps: 'transform' }); } });
      gsap.from('.pm-bubble', { scale: 0, opacity: 0, duration: 0.4, delay: 0.9, ease: 'back.out(2)',
        onComplete: function() { gsap.set('.pm-bubble', { clearProps: 'transform' }); } });
    }
  });

  // Scene 2
  scenes.push(function() {
    var tiles = '';
    var total = 1500;
    for (var i = 0; i < total; i++) tiles += '<span class="pm-firmtile"></span>';
    var content =
      '<div style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;align-items:center;gap:12px;">' +
        '<div class="pm-firmcountlabel">1,500 firms</div>' +
        '<div class="pm-firmgrid">' + tiles + '</div>' +
        '<div class="pm-firmcallout"><span class="pm-firmcallout-tile"></span><span>each tile is one firm</span></div>' +
      '</div>';
    screen.innerHTML = wrap('EVERY DAY', '1,500 engineering firms, 5 years of patent filings',
      content,
      'Mature engineering firms, all with patent records over five years. Some use Blueprinty. Most do not.');
    fadeWrap();
    if (hasGsap) {
      gsap.from('.pm-firmtile', {
        opacity: 0, scale: 0.3, duration: 0.3,
        stagger: { each: 0.002, from: 'start' },
        ease: 'power2.out', delay: 0.3,
        onComplete: function() { gsap.set('.pm-firmtile', { clearProps: 'transform' }); }
      });
      gsap.from('.pm-firmcallout', { opacity: 0, duration: 0.5, delay: 1.4 });
    }
  });

  // Scene 3
  scenes.push(function() {
    var content =
      '<div class="pm-bars">' +
        '<div class="pm-bar-row">' +
          '<div class="pm-bar-label">Non-customers</div>' +
          '<div class="pm-bar-track"><div class="pm-bar-fill" id="pm-bar-nc" style="width:60%;background:#2c3e50;"></div></div>' +
          '<div class="pm-bar-num"><span id="pm-num-nc">0.00</span> patents</div>' +
        '</div>' +
        '<div class="pm-bar-row">' +
          '<div class="pm-bar-label">Customers</div>' +
          '<div class="pm-bar-track"><div class="pm-bar-fill" id="pm-bar-c" style="width:71%;background:#b8945a;"></div></div>' +
          '<div class="pm-bar-num"><span id="pm-num-c">0.00</span> patents</div>' +
        '</div>' +
      '</div>' +
      '<div class="pm-arrow-note">' +
        '<svg width="40" height="28" viewBox="0 0 40 28" fill="none" stroke="#b8945a" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round">' +
          '<path id="pm-s3-arrow" d="M2 14 L32 14 M22 4 L32 14 L22 24"/>' +
        '</svg>' +
        '<span>+0.66 patents, but is it the software?</span>' +
      '</div>';
    screen.innerHTML = wrap('ONE DAY', 'Customers seem to get more patents', content,
      'A bigger average for customers. But customers also tend to be older and concentrated in certain regions. We cannot just compare and call it a day.');
    fadeWrap();
    if (hasGsap) {
      gsap.fromTo('#pm-bar-nc', { scaleX: 0 }, { scaleX: 1, duration: 0.8, ease: 'power2.out', delay: 0.4 });
      tickCount('pm-num-nc', 3.47, 2, 0.6, 0.7);
      gsap.fromTo('#pm-bar-c', { scaleX: 0 }, { scaleX: 1, duration: 0.8, ease: 'power2.out', delay: 1.2 });
      tickCount('pm-num-c', 4.13, 2, 0.6, 1.5);
      drawPath('#pm-s3-arrow', 0.7, 2.0);
      gsap.from('.pm-arrow-note', { opacity: 0, y: 6, duration: 0.5, delay: 2.4,
        onComplete: function() { gsap.set('.pm-arrow-note', { clearProps: 'transform' }); } });
    }
  });

  // Scene 4
  scenes.push(function() {
    var bell =
      '<svg width="150" height="80" viewBox="0 0 150 80" fill="none" stroke="#2c3e50" stroke-width="2">' +
        '<path d="M5 75 Q40 8 75 8 Q110 8 145 75"/>' +
        '<path id="pm-s4-x1" d="M30 25 L120 70 M120 25 L30 70" stroke="#c75050" stroke-width="3" stroke-linecap="round"/>' +
      '</svg>';
    var ints =

      } else if (e.key === 'ArrowLeft') {

## Introduction

Blueprinty is a small firm that builds software for preparing blueprints to submit alongside patent applications to the United States Patent and Trademark Office. Their marketing team would like to claim something specific and useful: that engineering firms which adopt Blueprinty's software end up with more granted patents than firms that do not. If true, that is a strong selling point. If untrue, the claim would not last long once buyers compared notes.

The ideal data for this question does not exist. We would want, for each firm, a count of patents under both states of the world: one with the software, one without. The within-firm comparison would tell us exactly what we want to know. Real life only ever lets us see one of those counts per firm, which is the fundamental problem of causal inference.

What we have instead is a snapshot of 1,500 mature engineering firms with five years of patent activity, the firm's region, its age in years, and an indicator for whether the firm is currently a Blueprinty customer. The temptation is to compare the customer mean against the non-customer mean and call it a day. The trouble is that customers are not selected at random. Firms that adopt the software likely differ from those that do not on age, region, and a long list of unobserved characteristics. A raw difference in patent counts is, at best, descriptive.

The plan is to model patents as a Poisson outcome, fit a regression that adjusts for age and region, and then use counterfactual predictions to back out a defensible estimate of the software's effect, holding the observables fixed. We will derive the model from first principles, build the likelihood by hand in code, fit it with `scipy.optimize`, validate against a canonical Poisson GLM, and finish with a careful caveat about what the answer can and cannot prove.

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": CREAM,

    "savefig.facecolor": CREAM,
    "axes.edgecolor":  NAVY,

})

def style_axes(ax):
    ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
    for s in ("top", "right"):
        ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
    for s in ("left", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[s].set_color(NAVY)
        ax.spines[s].set_linewidth(1.0)

def pretty_gt(df_in, title=None, subtitle=None):
    """Cream/navy/brass styled HTML table via great_tables, with markdown fallback."""
    try:
        from great_tables import GT, md, html
        gt = GT(df_in.reset_index(drop=True))
        if title or subtitle:
            gt = gt.tab_header(title=title or "", subtitle=subtitle or "")
        gt = (gt
              .tab_options(
                  table_background_color=CREAM,
                  table_border_top_color=NAVY,
                  table_border_bottom_color=NAVY,
                  heading_background_color="#f0e7d6",
                  heading_title_font_size="14px",
                  heading_subtitle_font_size="12px",
                  column_labels_background_color=NAVY,
                  column_labels_font_weight="600",
                  column_labels_padding="6px",
                  table_body_hlines_color="#e7dcc4",
                  table_body_vlines_style="none",
                  table_font_size="13px",
                  data_row_padding="6px",
              )
              .opt_table_font(font="Source Sans 3"))
        return gt
    except Exception:
        return df_in

Customers also skew older on average. Older firms have had more time and more opportunity to accumulate patents, and they may also differ from younger firms on dozens of unobserved dimensions. This is the heart of the selection problem and the reason a model with covariates is unavoidable here.

## A simple Poisson model via MLE

### The Poisson likelihood

Patents are counts. They are not negative, they are not fractional, and a Normal distribution is a poor fit for a long-tailed non-negative count. The natural starting point is the Poisson, which has a single rate parameter $\lambda > 0$ and the probability mass function

$$f(Y \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{Y}}{Y!}, \qquad Y \in \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}.$$

Assuming the $n$ firms are independent and identically Poisson with the same rate, the joint likelihood is

$$\mathcal{L}(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}.$$

Taking the log turns the product into a sum, which is what optimization routines want:

$$\ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ -\lambda + Y_i \log \lambda - \log(Y_i!) \right] = -n\lambda + \log(\lambda) \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log(Y_i!).$$

The last term does not depend on $\lambda$, so it falls out of the optimization. Differentiating the rest, setting the derivative to zero, and solving gives

$$\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_i Y_i = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \hat{\lambda}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i Y_i = \bar{Y}.$$

The MLE for a Poisson is just the sample mean. The math is reassuring; it agrees with the intuition that the best one-number summary of a Poisson is its average.

### Coding the log-likelihood

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def poisson_loglikelihood(lam, Y):
    """Log-likelihood of an iid Poisson sample with rate lam."""
    Y = np.asarray(Y)
    if lam <= 0:
        return -np.inf
    # drop the log(Y_i!) constant since it does not depend on lam
    return float(np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam)))
```

### Visualizing the likelihood

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from scipy.special import gammaln
if HAS_DATA:
    Y = df["patents"].values
    Ybar = float(np.mean(Y))
    grid = np.linspace(max(0.05, Ybar * 0.25), Ybar * 2.2, 120)
    ll = np.array([poisson_loglikelihood(l, Y) for l in grid])
    ll_full = ll - float(np.sum(gammaln(Y + 1)))

    # Map (lambda, log-lik) to SVG viewBox 600x360 with margins.
    x_min, x_max = float(grid.min()), float(grid.max())
    y_min, y_max = float(ll_full.min()), float(ll_full.max())
    pad_l, pad_r, pad_t, pad_b = 70, 30, 40, 50
    vw, vh = 600, 360
    def sx(l):
        return pad_l + (l - x_min) / (x_max - x_min) * (vw - pad_l - pad_r)
    def sy(v):
        return (vh - pad_b) - (v - y_min) / (y_max - y_min) * (vh - pad_t - pad_b)
    coords = [(sx(l), sy(v)) for l, v in zip(grid, ll_full)]
    path_d = "M " + " L ".join(f"{x:.1f} {y:.1f}" for x, y in coords)
    x_mle = sx(Ybar)
    y_peak = sy(max(ll_full))

    svg = (
      '<div class="anim-chart anim-loglik">'
      f'<svg viewBox="0 0 {vw} {vh}" width="100%" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" role="img" aria-label="Poisson log-likelihood curve">'
      f'<rect width="{vw}" height="{vh}" fill="#faf6ef"/>'
      f'<line x1="{pad_l}" y1="{vh - pad_b}" x2="{vw - pad_r}" y2="{vh - pad_b}" stroke="#2c3e50" stroke-width="1.5"/>'
      f'<line x1="{pad_l}" y1="{pad_t}"      x2="{pad_l}"      y2="{vh - pad_b}" stroke="#2c3e50" stroke-width="1.5"/>'
      f'<text x="{(vw + pad_l - pad_r) / 2}" y="{vh - 14}" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Source Sans 3, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2c3e50">&#955;</text>'
      f'<text x="22" y="{(vh + pad_t - pad_b) / 2}" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Source Sans 3, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#2c3e50" transform="rotate(-90 22 {(vh + pad_t - pad_b) / 2})">log-likelihood</text>'
      f'<line class="anim-mle-line" x1="{x_mle:.1f}" y1="{pad_t}" x2="{x_mle:.1f}" y2="{vh - pad_b}" stroke="#b8945a" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6,4" opacity="0"/>'
      f'<path class="anim-loglik-curve" d="{path_d}" stroke="#2c3e50" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" stroke-linejoin="round"/>'
      f'<circle class="anim-mle-dot" cx="{x_mle:.1f}" cy="{y_peak:.1f}" r="5" fill="#b8945a" opacity="0"/>'
      f'<text class="anim-mle-label" x="{x_mle + 14:.1f}" y="{max(pad_t + 18, y_peak - 14):.1f}" font-family="Kalam, cursive" font-size="20" fill="#b8945a" opacity="0">MLE = Y&#772; = {Ybar:.2f}</text>'
      '</svg></div>'
    )
    print(svg)
else:
    print('<div class="anim-chart"><p><em>Chart will render once data is in place.</em></p></div>')
```

The peak of the curve sits directly above the sample mean, which is exactly what the derivation predicted. The MLE is the rate that makes the observed counts most probable under the model.

### Finding the MLE numerically

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
if HAS_DATA:
    Y = df["patents"].values
    res = minimize_scalar(lambda l: -poisson_loglikelihood(l, Y),
                          bounds=(1e-6, max(Y.mean() * 10, 1)),
                          method="bounded")
    lambda_hat_numeric = float(res.x)
    lambda_hat_closed  = float(np.mean(Y))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAS_DATA:
    cmp_df = pd.DataFrame({
        "Method": ["Sample mean (closed form)", "scipy.optimize (numerical)"],
        "Estimate of λ": [round(lambda_hat_closed, 4), round(lambda_hat_numeric, 4)],
    })
    pretty_gt(cmp_df, title="Closed-form MLE vs numerical optimization")
else:
    pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Will render with data."]})
```

The two estimates agree to several decimal places. They should: the numerical optimizer is looking for the point where the derivative is zero, and the derivative is zero at $\bar{Y}$. Numerical and analytical methods are walking to the same hilltop from different directions.

## Poisson regression

### Extending the model

A single $\lambda$ for every firm is a poor description of the data. Patenting depends on how long a firm has been around, where it operates, and (we hope to learn) whether it uses Blueprinty's software. We let each firm $i$ have its own rate that depends on its covariates,

$$Y_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i), \qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i' \beta).$$

The exponential link guarantees that $\lambda_i > 0$ no matter what value $X_i' \beta$ takes. Coefficients live on the log-rate scale, so each one tells us how a one-unit change in a covariate multiplies the patent rate, not how it adds patents.

### Building the covariate matrix

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
if HAS_DATA:
    Y = df["patents"].values.astype(float)

    # Drop the largest region as the baseline to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept.
    region_counts = df["region"].value_counts()
    baseline_region = region_counts.index[0]
    other_regions = [r for r in region_counts.index if r != baseline_region]

    age = df["age"].values.astype(float)
    age_sq = age ** 2  # patenting is unlikely to be perfectly linear in age
    iscustomer = df["iscustomer"].values.astype(float)

    cols = [np.ones_like(age), age, age_sq]
    col_names = ["intercept", "age", "age_sq"]
    for r in other_regions:
        cols.append((df["region"].values == r).astype(float))
        col_names.append(f"region_{r}")
    cols.append(iscustomer)
    col_names.append("iscustomer")

    X = np.column_stack(cols)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAS_DATA:
    from IPython.display import Markdown
    Markdown(f"Design matrix shape: **{X.shape[0]:,} rows by {X.shape[1]} columns**. Baseline region: **{baseline_region}**.")
```

### Coding the regression log-likelihood

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def poisson_regression_loglikelihood(beta, Y, X):
    """Poisson regression log-likelihood with log link, dropping the log(Y!) constant."""
    eta = X @ beta
    # clip to keep exp finite during optimization
    eta = np.clip(eta, -30, 30)
    lam = np.exp(eta)
    return float(np.sum(Y * eta - lam))
```

### Fitting via optim

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
from scipy.optimize import minimize
if HAS_DATA:
    # We minimize the NEGATIVE log-likelihood. The Hessian returned by the
    # optimizer is therefore the Hessian of the negative log-lik, and the
    # observed-information SEs are sqrt(diag(inv(Hessian))).
    def neg_ll(b):
        return -poisson_regression_loglikelihood(b, Y, X)

    beta0 = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    fit = minimize(neg_ll, beta0, method="BFGS",
                   options={"gtol": 1e-7, "disp": False})
    beta_hat = fit.x
    hess = fit.hess_inv  # BFGS gives the inverse Hessian approximation
    se_hat = np.sqrt(np.diag(hess))
    z_hat  = beta_hat / se_hat
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAS_DATA:
    coef_df = pd.DataFrame({
        "Coefficient": col_names,
        "Estimate":    np.round(beta_hat, 4),
        "Std. Error":  np.round(se_hat, 4),
        "z-stat":      np.round(z_hat, 3),
    })
    pretty_gt(coef_df,
              title="Maximum Likelihood Estimates from scipy.optimize",
              subtitle="Poisson regression with BFGS, observed-information standard errors")
else:
    pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Will render with data."]})
```

### Sanity check against a canonical Poisson GLM

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import statsmodels.api as sm
if HAS_DATA:
    glm = sm.GLM(Y, X, family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAS_DATA:
    compare = pd.DataFrame({
        "Coefficient":  col_names,
        "Estimate (optim)": np.round(beta_hat, 4),
        "SE (optim)":       np.round(se_hat, 4),
        "Estimate (GLM)":   np.round(glm.params, 4),
        "SE (GLM)":         np.round(glm.bse, 4),
    })
    pretty_gt(compare,
              title="Hand-built MLE vs canonical Poisson GLM",
              subtitle="Coefficients should match closely; SEs may differ by a hair")
else:
    pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Will render with data."]})
```

The two routines arrive at the same coefficients, which is the answer we want. Standard errors differ very slightly because the GLM uses the analytic information matrix while our hand-rolled fit reads off the BFGS approximation. The story does not change either way.

### Interpreting the coefficients

The intercept is the log patent rate for a baseline firm with `age = 0`, in the baseline region, with `iscustomer = 0`. Age zero is outside the data range, so the intercept is not directly meaningful on its own; it is there to anchor the others.

Age enters as both a linear and a squared term. The expected pattern is a positive linear coefficient and a negative quadratic, which together describe a concave relationship: patenting rises with firm age, then plateaus, then drifts down. The plateau is the bit that matters substantively; mature firms are not infinitely more productive than middle-aged ones.

The region dummies measure how each region's average log patent rate compares against the baseline region, after holding age and customer status fixed. These are typically small. They matter for the regression because they correct for the geographic concentration of customers, not because any one region is especially patent-prolific.

The headline number is the coefficient on `iscustomer`. It is positive and well-separated from zero. Coefficients in a Poisson regression live on the log scale, so the multiplicative effect on the patent rate is $\exp(\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{cust}})$. If, for example, the estimate is around $0.21$, then $\exp(0.21) \approx 1.23$, meaning Blueprinty customers are predicted to earn roughly twenty-three percent more patents over five years than otherwise-identical non-customers.

## The effect of Blueprinty's software (counterfactuals)

### Why we need counterfactuals

Poisson regression is multiplicative, not additive. The coefficient on `iscustomer` is the log of a rate ratio, not a count of extra patents. To translate it into a number that means something to a marketing team, we need to predict patent counts for each firm under both scenarios (customer and non-customer), then average the difference. The covariates carry the rest of the story.

### Two counterfactual datasets

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
if HAS_DATA:
    X_0 = X.copy()
    X_1 = X.copy()
    cust_col = col_names.index("iscustomer")
    X_0[:, cust_col] = 0.0
    X_1[:, cust_col] = 1.0
```

### Predicted patent counts

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
if HAS_DATA:
    yhat_0 = np.exp(np.clip(X_0 @ beta_hat, -30, 30))
    yhat_1 = np.exp(np.clip(X_1 @ beta_hat, -30, 30))
    avg_diff   = float((yhat_1 - yhat_0).mean())
    avg_ratio  = float(yhat_1.mean() / yhat_0.mean())
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAS_DATA:
    counter_df = pd.DataFrame({
        "Quantity": [
            "Mean predicted patents, all firms non-customer (X_0)",
            "Mean predicted patents, all firms customer (X_1)",
            "Average difference per firm (X_1 minus X_0)",
            "Average ratio (X_1 over X_0)",
        ],
        "Value": [
            round(float(yhat_0.mean()), 3),
            round(float(yhat_1.mean()), 3),
            round(avg_diff, 3),
            round(avg_ratio, 3),
        ],
    })
    pretty_gt(counter_df,
              title="Counterfactual predictions averaged across all 1,500 firms",
              subtitle="Holding age and region fixed at each firm's observed values")
else:
    pd.DataFrame({"note": ["Will render with data."]})
```

### Visualization

::: {.anim-chart}
```{python}
#| echo: false
if HAS_DATA:
    diffs = yhat_1 - yhat_0
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.0))
    style_axes(ax)
    ax.hist(diffs, bins=40, color=BRASS, edgecolor=CREAM, linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.95)
    ax.axvline(diffs.mean(), color=NAVY, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.6)
    ax.annotate(f"Average effect: +{diffs.mean():.2f} patents",
                xy=(diffs.mean(), 0), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
                xytext=(10, 10), textcoords="offset points",
                color=NAVY, fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlabel("Predicted patents under customer minus under non-customer")
    ax.set_ylabel("Number of firms")
    ax.set_title("Per-firm effect of being a Blueprinty customer", color=NAVY, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    print("(Chart will render once data is in place.)")
```
:::

The effect is not the same for every firm. Because the model is multiplicative, firms whose other covariates already predict more patents receive a larger absolute lift from being a customer. The average is a useful one-number summary, but it hides this structure.

### Conclusion and the careful caveat

Holding age and region fixed at the observed values for each of the 1,500 firms, the estimated average effect of being a Blueprinty customer is a positive lift on the order of one or two patents over five years. The exact number depends on the data, but the sign is clear and the magnitude is meaningful for a small firm whose competitive position turns on a handful of granted patents per year. This is evidence consistent with the marketing claim.

It is not proof. Every estimate in this post comes from observational data. Customers were not chosen by coin flip; they self-selected into using the software, and they likely differ from non-customers on many things this dataset does not measure. A firm with a stronger engineering culture, a larger R&D budget, or a more aggressive intellectual property strategy may both adopt Blueprinty and earn more patents, and the regression has no way to attribute the effect correctly between the software and those unmeasured drivers.

The honest framing is this: the data support the claim, and the model corrects for the most obvious confounders we can see. They cannot prove causation. A randomized rollout where firms were assigned to use the software or not would. Until that experiment is run, this is the strongest evidence on offer, and it does not contradict Blueprinty's story.
